name: kyrle disease
aliases: hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis in cutem penetrans

clinicalPearls: A perforating dermatosis characterised by large keratotic papules and nodules with a central horny plug, typically on the lower limbs, and often only mildly pruritic compared with other perforating disorders.
Classically described in adults with chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus or hepatic dysfunction, overlapping clinically with acquired perforating dermatosis.
Lesions may coalesce into verrucous plaques and characteristically follow a Koebner (isomorphic) distribution along scratch lines.
Histology shows a keratotic plug filling an epidermal invagination with a parakeratotic column and focal perforation through the epidermis, with basophilic connective-tissue debris in the plug.

In classic Kyrle disease the perforating channel is said not to specifically eliminate collagen or elastic fibres, distinguishing it from reactive perforating collagenosis and elastosis perforans serpiginosa, though overlap is common.
Diagnosis rests on correlating the clinical picture (keratotic plugged papules on legs of a patient with renal or metabolic disease) with the perforating histology.
Treatment mirrors other acquired perforating dermatoses: emollients, keratolytics, topical or oral retinoids, phototherapy, and control of the underlying systemic disease.
A rare familial form with childhood onset and no systemic association is described, but most cases are acquired in adulthood.
reference.pathophysiology: Kyrle disease is regarded by many authorities as a variant within the acquired perforating dermatosis spectrum. The primary abnormality is thought to be a focal disturbance of epidermal keratinisation producing a keratotic plug and a clone of abnormally differentiating keratinocytes that accelerates upward, breaching the basement membrane and perforating the epidermis. Basophilic degenerate connective-tissue debris accumulates within the plug and is eliminated transepidermally. In acquired cases, metabolic derangements of uraemia, diabetes and hepatic disease, together with microangiopathy and repetitive scratch-induced trauma (Koebnerisation), are believed to trigger the aberrant keratinisation and perforation.
additionalDifferentials: keratosis pilaris and other follicular keratoses
additionalInvestigations: skin biopsy of an intact keratotic papule to demonstrate the epidermal invagination, parakeratotic plug and perforation
renal function tests and estimated glomerular filtration rate
redFlags: presentation without recognised renal, hepatic or metabolic disease, warranting systemic evaluation
features suggesting secondary infection of excoriated lesions
rapid enlargement of a solitary nodule raising concern for keratoacanthoma or squamous cell carcinoma
intractable pruritus indicating uncontrolled uraemia or hyperglycaemia
reference.prognosis: The course is chronic with a tendency to relapse; individual lesions may resolve leaving scars or hyperpigmentation, and overall activity generally parallels control of the underlying systemic disease.
pitfalls: labelling any leg-predominant perforating eruption as Kyrle disease without histological correlation, given substantial overlap with other perforating dermatoses
overlooking the need to screen for chronic kidney disease, diabetes and hepatic dysfunction
mistaking a coalescent verrucous plaque for a viral wart or squamous neoplasm
sampling a superinfected or excoriated lesion, which distorts the characteristic histology
management: Optimise treatment of the underlying systemic disorder - adequate dialysis and management of chronic kidney disease, tight glycaemic control in diabetes and treatment of hepatic disease - as skin activity parallels this
Apply topical keratolytics such as urea, salicylic acid or topical retinoids together with topical corticosteroids to individual lesions
Control pruritus with emollients and oral antihistamines to interrupt the itch-scratch cycle and reduce Koebnerisation
Consider narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy for widespread disease
Use systemic retinoids as a second-line option for resistant, extensive lesions
Provide wound care and monitor lesions for secondary infection
Refer to dermatology and coordinate with nephrology or the relevant specialty managing the systemic disease
